title: The US Just Proposed a 12.5% Forced Labour Tariff on India. The Trade Deal Was 99% Done.
excerpt: A 92-page USTR report accuses India of failing to block imports made with forced labour, threatening to derail the final round of bilateral trade talks in New Delhi
body:
The timing could not have been more pointed. On the second day of critical trade talks in New Delhi, the office of the United States Trade Representative released a 92-page report proposing a 12.5 per cent tariff on Indian imports — not over market access or intellectual property, but over forced labour.

India, the USTR said, is among 54 economies that lack a forced-labour import prohibition and have therefore "failed to impose and effectively enforce" protections against goods made with coerced workers entering their markets. The proposal, filed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, lands squarely in the middle of what both governments have described as the final stretch of their first-ever bilateral trade agreement.

## The Accusation

"The failure of our most important trading partners to address the importation of goods made with forced labour is unacceptable," USTR Jamieson Greer said in a statement accompanying the report. "This creates a dynamic where American workers are forced to compete globally on an unlevel playing field."

The report goes further. It identifies India as an intermediary in cotton supply chains linked to Chinese forced-labour inputs — a reference to Xinjiang cotton that has been central to Washington's economic confrontation with Beijing for years. The implication is that Chinese cotton processed in Indian textile mills and re-exported to the United States is circumventing American forced-labour import bans.

India's commerce ministry did not immediately respond. But the report's framing is significant: the investigation is not about forced labour in Indian exports. It is about whether India blocks imports made with forced labour elsewhere — a distinction that trade experts say could be challenged.

## A Deal That Was 99 Per Cent Done

The tariff proposal arrives at a particularly delicate moment. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said just two days ago that 99 per cent of the India-US bilateral trade agreement had been finalised. US Ambassador Sergio Gore confirmed that figure. The American delegation, led by Assistant USTR Brendan Lynch, is currently in New Delhi through June 4 for what was billed as the final negotiating round.

The agreement covers market access, non-tariff measures, customs facilitation, investment promotion, and economic security alignment. India had committed to purchasing $500 billion worth of American energy products, aircraft, and technology over five years — a headline figure designed to demonstrate reciprocity.

An Indian government source told Reuters that New Delhi planned to raise the Section 301 investigation directly with Lynch's team, seeking tariff relief as part of the broader deal. India is also seeking preferential tariff treatment over competing manufacturing hubs in South and Southeast Asia.

## The Pressure Tactic Theory

Ajay Srivastava, founder of the Global Trade Research Initiative, offered a blunt assessment. "The proposed tariffs are viewed as part of broader US pressure tactics," he said, arguing that India should treat Section 301 actions and the bilateral trade agreement negotiations separately.

The forced-labour tariff framework creates a two-tier system: 54 nations without import prohibitions face 12.5 per cent, while six others — including Canada, the EU, Indonesia, and Mexico — that have prohibitions but allegedly fail to enforce them face a lower 10 per cent levy.

For India's textile and apparel sector, which exports roughly $9 billion annually to the United States, the implications are direct. If the tariff is imposed, Indian garment exports would become significantly less competitive against Bangladesh, Vietnam, and other suppliers that may negotiate exemptions through the bilateral deal framework.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the more than 4.4 million Indian Americans and the businesses that depend on India-US trade corridors, the stakes are tangible. The bilateral trade in goods and services has surged from $20 billion to over $220 billion in two decades. An additional 12.5 per cent tariff layer, even if narrowly applied, would ripple through supply chains, investment flows, and the cost structures of Indian-American businesses with manufacturing ties to India.

The next 48 hours in New Delhi will determine whether the forced-labour report is a negotiating lever that gets folded into the broader deal — or the beginning of a longer and more contentious trade confrontation.
author: Diaspora Desk
